freshness_notes.ofcom_connected_nations_spring: published 13 May 2026; snapshot as of January 2026
freshness_notes.ofcom_planned_network_deployments: published 13 May 2026; plans to end-2028 based on January 2026 operator submissions
freshness_notes.ons_private_rent_house_prices: published 22 July 2026; rents through June 2026 and HPI through May 2026

batches.c: Ofcom Spring 2026 is a January 2026 coverage snapshot. Candidate use requires exact premise/address coverage; local-authority coverage percentages are context only.
Full-fibre availability and take-up measure different things. Area take-up cannot be converted into site demand or connection certainty without exact premise/provider evidence.
Current gigabit-capable coverage is network availability evidence, not a guarantee of service at the candidate. Exact premise checker/provider result is required.
Ofcom reports mobile coverage with confidence conventions. Local or national percentages cannot prove indoor/outdoor coverage at a candidate coordinate.
5G standalone and non-standalone coverage are distinct. Candidate connectivity must preserve technology/status and exact location evidence.
USO-related thresholds and availability are premise-specific and can be affected by alternative technologies. Area statistics are not an eligibility decision.
Ofcom planned deployment data are operator plans, including confidence states, not current service. Planned coverage is never promoted as present parcel connectivity.
High-confidence network plans use design/funding criteria but remain future delivery evidence. Exact build completion and premise service availability are required.
BDUK contract reporting separates contracted and built premises. Contract coverage does not prove a candidate has been built or activated.
BDUK open-market reviews collect current and planned gigabit infrastructure. Planned commercial build is not current connectivity and exact premise matching remains required.
HMLR Price Paid Data records qualifying completed sales lodged for registration. Candidate value use requires an exact property/address match; nearby sales are comparables only.
PPD excludes some transaction types and depends on registration. Missing or delayed records are not proof that no transaction occurred.
UK HPI provides aggregate local-authority price estimates. It is market context, not a valuation for an individual parcel or development.
Recent HPI estimates are provisional and can be revised as more transactions arrive. Candidate context must preserve publication month and revision status.
ONS PIPR provides local-area rent levels and inflation. These are area demand signals, not achievable rent for a proposed unit without scheme-level evidence.
Rent price level and annual inflation measure different market dimensions. Neither is a parcel-level rent appraisal without comparable property evidence.
Affordability combines area house prices and earnings. It can indicate demand pressure but does not prove viability or sales value for a candidate.
ONS neighbourhood affordability uses MSOA prices with local-authority earnings. Exact candidate-to-MSOA binding is required before using the statistic as local context.
Small-area house-price measures depend on transaction samples and geography. Sparse transactions can make local movements volatile and must not be over-weighted.
Monthly HPI and rent measures can fluctuate and be revised. Growth scoring must use longer-term context rather than a single monthly movement.

batches.t: Net additional dwellings local-authority delivery gate
batches.c: Annual net additions are the comprehensive authority-level housing supply measure. They indicate delivery context, not parcel deliverability.
Net additions combine new build, conversions, change of use, other gains and demolitions. Component mix must be preserved when interpreting local growth.
Quarterly building-control starts are a timely leading indicator but not equivalent to planning permissions or future completions on a candidate site.
Quarterly completions measure recent delivery and can differ from annual net additions. They remain area-level delivery evidence.
MHCLG uses new EPC lodgements as a proxy for recent net supply with adjustments. Proxy estimates are not exact site completion records.
Dwelling stock provides the denominator for supply-rate comparisons. Stock size/density cannot determine development capacity of an individual parcel.
Dwellings per hectare is an area density statistic. It does not establish acceptable site density without planning/design/constraint evidence.
Vacancy tables can inform local housing-market context, but vacant-stock levels do not establish demand, availability or viability for a candidate development.
Bulk EPC data can support exact property matching where a valid certificate/address exists. Certificate evidence must be tied to the actual property and current certificate.
Bulk EPC records can include expired or superseded certificates. The latest valid property record must be resolved before any energy-performance conclusion.
Local EPC distributions indicate existing-stock efficiency. They do not predict the rating of a future scheme without its design specification.
Non-domestic EPC data can contextualise commercial stock, but exact building/use matching is required and it cannot be transferred to undeveloped land.
Weekly EPC lodgements are a rapid activity indicator for new/existing dwellings. They are not planning permissions and can be revised or duplicated by replacement certificates.
NEED consumption tables describe household energy use statistically. They support demand/efficiency context but are not parcel-specific utility-load evidence.
ASHE workplace earnings provide local labour-market context. Sampling uncertainty and geography mean the figures cannot be treated as scheme-specific household income.
Residence-based earnings differ from workplace earnings because of commuting. Affordability/demand interpretation must keep the two concepts separate.
Workforce jobs are a short-term jobs measure compiled from multiple sources. Regional/industry job change is context, not proof of employment growth at a candidate site.
ONS business demography records enterprise creations and closures, including low-level geography. It is area business dynamism evidence, not a parcel-specific occupier forecast.
